before: Abstract—  Electronic nose  calibration usually relies on controlled gas exposures with known concentrations. In practice, however, unlabeled responses are much easier to collect because they carry no concentration annotation. The present experiments reuse controlled exposures with their concentration labels withheld during pretraining, so they demonstrate reduced labeled-calibration requirements rather than reduced gas-generation cost. This study explores whether those unlabeled measurements can be useful before the calibration stage through sensor-aware self-supervised learning. The proposed model uses a shared dilated one-dimensional convolutional encoder to learn temporal behavior. Sensor embeddings preserve channel identity, while attention captures relationships across the array. During pretraining, the model reconstructs masked time spans and complete sensor channels. The resulting encoder is then adapted using a limited number of concentration labels. The evaluation includes a private 20-channel NH3/H2 array, a public 16-channel CO/ethylene array, and a public 36-month sensor drift dataset. At the full label budget, transfer achieves mean absolute errors of 14.92 ppm for NH3, 29.16 ppm for H2, 46.16 ppm for CO, and 1.371 ppm for ethylene. These results correspond to gains of 19.2%, 20.3%, 29.0%, and 31.2% over scratch training. The benefit generally becomes larger when fewer labels are available. On sensor drift dataset, oracle-class gas-conditional concentration error decreases in three future partitions by 17.3%, 29.9%, and 2.8%. Quantitative transfer therefore retains some within-gas concentration information under long-term drift, although the benefit decreases under the strongest future shift.
after: Abstract— Precisely labeled gas mixtures require concentration control or reference quantification, whereas mixtures without carefully controlled ppm can provide inexpensive unlabeled sensor responses. This motivates self-supervised pretraining on a large unquantified mixture pool followed by calibration with a small precisely labeled set. We evaluate the label-efficiency premise using existing datasets with concentration labels withheld during pretraining. A shared temporal encoder, sensor-identity embeddings, cross-sensor attention, and structured masked reconstruction are evaluated with a predefined fine-tuned transfer policy and 10 seeds. Primary evaluation uses six held-partition NH3/H2 folds and three rolling chronological CO/ethylene folds. Relative MAE reductions against scratch are NH3 13.9%, H2 21.5%, CO 27.5%, Ethylene 25.7%. Paired seed-and-fold bootstrap intervals exclude zero for these four comparisons, conditional on the observed exposures. Fixed-split experiments compare all adaptation policies, calibration designs, classical regression, a compact PatchTST-style SSL control, architectural ablations, and window placement. The proposed architecture is not uniformly superior to generic SSL or classical models. Long-term drift evaluation includes constant controls, normalized errors, small budgets, and target-loss sensitivity; regression is conditional on known gas identity. These results support label-efficient same-system recalibration. Prospective pretraining on cheaply acquired, unquantified mixtures and its cost savings remain to be evaluated.

after: The practical motivation is the cost difference between producing gas mixtures and establishing their precise gas-phase concentrations at the sensors. Mixtures prepared without carefully controlling ppm can supply inexpensive response recordings for self-supervised learning; only a small calibration set needs precise concentration labels. Source identities or preparation settings, when available, do not substitute for measured gas-phase ppm. The intended workflow therefore learns temporal response patterns and relationships among sensors from an unquantified mixture pool, then adapts the representation using precisely labeled calibration samples. In this study, existing controlled-exposure datasets with labels withheld during pretraining provide a retrospective test of that label-efficiency premise. They do not directly test a newly acquired low-cost mixture pool.

before: The encoder appears to learn more than a generic compression of the input. Sensor identity helps with several targets, which suggests that the physical channel index carries useful information. Complete-sensor masking is also beneficial in most cases, indicating that a missing response can be partly inferred from the remaining array. Full revision: The revised primary evidence supports lower mean MAE than scratch under the spec
after: The revised primary evidence supports lower mean MAE than scratch under the specified same-system protocols. It is more limited than a claim that sensor awareness is always beneficial: direct generic SSL and classical controls are competitive or stronger on several targets. The ablations show gas-dependent component effects, and the window study shows sensitivity to which part of an exposure is observed. These findings favor a calibrated assessment of the complete training procedure rather than attributing all benefits to physical sensor embeddings.

location: Full revision: Increasing from three to ten seeds does not systematically weaken the primary re
after: Increasing from three to ten seeds does not systematically weaken the primary result. H2 and NH3 reductions increase modestly; CO and ethylene attenuate slightly. Seeds vary model initialization/training, calibration design and adaptation holdouts. More seeds characterize this pipeline variability, but cannot substitute for independent acquisition sessions or additional devices. In particular, the NH3 multi-fold interval is close to zero, only three rolling CO/ethylene folds are available, and training partitions overlap across folds. The descriptive intervals and exploratory control comparisons should therefore not be read as population-wide guarantees.

location: Full revision: The secondary fixed-split benefits weaken more clearly with additional seeds, es
after: The secondary fixed-split benefits weaken more clearly with additional seeds, especially NH3. Thus the answer to seed stability depends on the evaluation: primary multi-fold advantages persist, while favorable single-split estimates from three seeds overstate several ten-seed effects. The drift audit is also partition-dependent, with no overall ten-seed benefit in partition 10. Reporting only the stable primary means would omit this sensitivity.

location: Full revision: The intended cost advantage comes from replacing much of a precisely quantified
after: The intended cost advantage comes from replacing much of a precisely quantified mixture collection with inexpensive response recordings from mixtures whose ppm need not be carefully controlled. The experiment tests the learning premise by withholding existing pretraining labels and measuring performance at limited adaptation-label budgets. It does not measure acquisition expenditure or establish that uncontrolled mixtures provide the same response coverage as the benchmark pool. A prospective test should pretrain on cheaply prepared unquantified mixtures, use a small precisely quantified adaptation set, and evaluate on separate quantified test exposures while accounting for all reference-measurement costs. Farthest-point calibration design uses known candidate concentrations, so its selected-pair budget cannot represent the total acquisition or labeling cost of that pool. Sensor-ID embeddings bind learned channel identities to the array layout; a cross-device evaluation would require compatible arrays and justified correspondence or embedding reinitialization. No such experiment is demonstrated here. Private sensor characterization and verification of physical exposure independence remain unresolved acquisition-record limitations.

location: Full revision: Long-term drift performance depends on the future partition, target transform, a
after: Long-term drift performance depends on the future partition, target transform, and gas. Constant prediction, per-gas normalization, tiny-budget controls, and the loss/scaling comparison prevent a small favorable macro-MAE difference from being treated as universal robustness. Explicit temporal/domain alignment and shift-aware uncertainty remain future work. The final claim is evidence for same-system representation reuse under a predefined adaptation policy, with documented failure modes and no universal-superiority or cross-device claim.

location: Section VI

location: Section VI

location: Section VI

after: The practical motivation is to learn from inexpensive mixture-response recordings and reserve precise concentration measurements for a small calibration set. Farthest-point design additionally requires known candidate concentrations, whose quantification cost is outside the selected-pair budget. Source and evidence status. The acquisition details below are translated and summarized from the author-supplied document Thu thập dữ liệu NH3_H2.docx, Sections 2.3.1-2.3.2 and its embedded setup/interface images. They supplement the deposited NH3/H2 dataset [29] (doi: 10.7910/DVN/LWUSKO). Reported settings are distinguished from verified file counts and unresolved discrepancies. The source is a descriptive acquisition account, not a timestamped per-exposure laboratory log; its internal citations [35] and [68] cannot be mapped to this manuscript bibliography from the supplied document.

Sensor array and readout. The source describes 20 MEMS metal-oxide channels based on nano-SnO2, with SnO2 nanowires surface-modified using Pt/Ag and a thermal-gradient sensing principle. It describes a 5 x 4 arrangement; the acquisition interface displays four groups of five channels (CH1-CH5, CH6-CH10, CH11-CH15 and CH16-CH20). Reported supply settings span 3.0-3.4 V; the screenshot shows 3.4, 3.2, 3.2 and 3.0 V. These are electrical settings, not measured heater temperatures. Manufacturer/model, channel-specific modifier assignments, fabrication details and heater-temperature calibration are not supplied.

Gas delivery and chamber. The acquisition account describes automated mass-flow-controlled mixing, a switching valve, a sensor chamber and an exhaust line. Its schematic shows air, NH3 and H2 supplies, an MFC interface, a power supply and a PC. The chamber photograph and accompanying text identify a 20-sensor assembly; another photograph shows the MFC installation. The software diagram labels the background stream Air/N2. The actual carrier gas used for each run, stock-gas concentrations/purity, MFC models and calibration, total/per-stream flow rates, chamber volume and reference-concentration uncertainty are not established by this account. The prose assigns NH3/H2 mixing to MFC1/MFC2, whereas the screenshot shows six controllers with different stream labels; exact controller-to-gas mapping therefore remains unresolved.

Exposure and recovery schedule. The reported cycle is 880 s: 180 s of gas response/exposure followed by 700 s of recovery/cleaning. The mixing-interface schedule also displays response and recovery entries of 180 and 700 s. The readout shows responses rising during gas delivery and returning toward a displayed baseline near 1 during recovery. This display does not define whether the stored response is R/R0, R0/R or another normalization, nor does it document the baseline-reference procedure or purge-gas identity.

Sampling and stored sequence length. The acquisition interface specifies Sampling time = 2.0 s and DataRate = 175 SPS, with Average sampling = 30 also visible. These are distinct interface settings: 175 SPS must not be presented as the stored time-series frequency without documentation of the acquisition/averaging chain. The account reports 429-430 stored rows per 880-s cycle. At a nominal 2-s interval, a full cycle would contain approximately 440 intervals, so start/stop timing, discarded rows or logging overhead require clarification. No timestamps or record-level mapping of these settings are supplied. Window definitions remain in sample coordinates rather than assuming an exact elapsed duration.

Mixture design and acquisition sessions. Both target concentrations span 0-500 ppm; nonzero programmed levels are 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 ppm. The design includes single-gas and binary-mixture conditions. The account states that a 63-condition protocol was repeated six times on six different measurement days, yielding 378 recorded sequences and 162,404 observations. Those totals agree with the deposited dataset and analysis. The six-day schedule is now documented as an author-reported protocol, but acquisition dates and a run-to-Combination/day mapping are absent. It does not independently establish that the six identifier-based analysis partitions correspond exactly to those days, or prove physical independence of all exposures.

Concentration-coordinate discrepancy. The source describes 63 combinations with 60 distinct concentration pairs. The processed-data audit used in this study identifies 57 unique (NH3,H2) coordinates within each 63-sequence partition, with six additional identifiers at repeated coordinates. These counts are not interchangeable. The source concentration-design table is referred to but is not present as a complete native table in the supplied document. Section 2.3.2 instead reports stable conditions of 25 degrees C and 82% RH. The supplied material does not identify different campaigns, locations, sensors or time periods that would reconcile these statements. Neither set is treated as a verified uniform condition for all analyzed records. The interface temperature display is not sufficient to identify chamber ambient temperature or sensor heater temperature. Humidity/temperature control equipment and per-run environmental logs are not described.

Record structure and remaining scope limits. The source states that each row has 13 features but enumerates one measurement identifier, two concentration fields and 20 sensor-response fields, which total 23 fields. The stated 13-field total is internally inconsistent; this study continues to use the 20 response channels and two concentration targets established by the processed data. The reported materials, timing and six-day acquisition plan improve documentation, but do not establish low-concentration ambient-monitoring performance, cross-device generalization, humidity robustness or reference-traceable concentration accuracy. The 0-500 ppm experiments remain a controlled calibration benchmark.

Digital leakage audit. The existing audit of 623 exposure/window identifiers found no identical stored-signal fingerprints or identifier overlap in 11 split definitions. CO/ethylene fingerprints cover cached windows rather than entire raw traces. These digital checks remain distinct from physical acquisition independence; the new six-day acquisition account does not replace timestamped run logs or alter any existing split, window, target or numerical result.

section_heading: NH3/H2 sensors, gas chamber and acquisition protocol
paragraphs: We use an array of 20 MEMS metal-oxide gas-sensor channels based on SnO2 nanowires with Pt/Ag surface modification. The sensors operate using a thermal-gradient sensing principle and provide complementary responses to NH3 and H2. The chamber accommodates the array in a 5 x 4 arrangement. We monitor the channels in four groups: CH1-CH5, CH6-CH10, CH11-CH15 and CH16-CH20, with electrical supply settings in the range 3.0-3.4 V.

We deliver NH3 and H2 to the sensor chamber through an automated mass-flow-controlled mixing system. The apparatus comprises gas supplies, background-gas delivery, mass-flow controllers, a switching valve, the sensor chamber, a power supply and a computer for control and recording. The switching valve directs the prepared mixture to the chamber during exposure. The outlet is connected to an exhaust line, and a cleaning-gas flow supports recovery between exposures. Figure S2 shows the system layout; Fig. S3 shows the sensor hardware, chamber assembly and mass-flow-controller installation.

We program a sequence of single-gas and binary NH3/H2 conditions spanning 0-500 ppm for each gas. Nonzero concentration settings are 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 ppm. For each condition, we expose the array to the prepared gas mixture for 180 s, then apply a 700-s recovery period, giving an 880-s measurement cycle. We record the multichannel responses throughout exposure and recovery, using a nominal 2.0-s sampling setting in the acquisition interface. The response increases during gas delivery and returns toward its baseline during recovery. We repeat the acquisition protocol on six separate measurement days. The computer interface controls the programmed sequence and records the response channels for subsequent concentration-regression analysis.

location: Main paragraph 6
before: lectronic nose systems infer gas properties from the combined response of partially selective sensors. For concentration estimation, they are normally calibrated through controlled exposures with known compositions. Obtaining precise concentration labels through controlled delivery or reference measurement becomes costly as the number of gases, mixtures, and measurement sessions grows. Moreover, aging sensors may require the calibration process to be repeated.
after: lectronic noses estimate gas properties from partially selective sensor arrays. Precise concentration labels require controlled delivery or reference measurement, making calibration costly across gases, mixtures and sessions. Sensor aging can require repeated calibration.

location: Main paragraph 7
before: The practical motivation is the cost difference between producing gas mixtures and establishing their precise gas-phase concentrations at the sensors. Mixtures prepared without carefully controlling ppm can supply inexpensive response recordings for self-supervised learning; only a small calibration set needs precise concentration labels. Source identities or preparation settings, when available, do not substitute for measured gas-phase ppm. The intended workflow therefore learns temporal response patterns and relationships among sensors from an unquantified mixture pool, then adapts the representation using precisely labeled calibration samples. In this study, existing controlled-exposure datasets with labels withheld during pretraining provide a retrospective test of that label-efficiency premise. They do not directly test a newly acquired low-cost mixture pool.
after: We seek to learn from inexpensive mixture-response recordings and reserve precise concentration measurements for a small calibration set. Preparation settings do not substitute for measured gas-phase ppm. Controlled-exposure datasets with labels withheld during pretraining test this premise retrospectively; they do not establish the cost or performance of a prospectively acquired unquantified mixture pool.

location: Main paragraph 8
before: Several earlier studies have already made use of limited or unlabeled electronic nose data. M-Training [1] and M-S4VMs [2], for example, use pseudo-labeling for gas recognition. Drift research has taken other directions, including domain adaptation, few-shot learning, and meta-learning [3]–[7]. Quantitative calibration appears less often in this literature, even though it is important for monitoring applications.
after: Limited-label electronic-nose research includes pseudo-labeling for recognition [1], [2] and domain adaptation, few-shot learning and meta-learning for drift [3]-[7]. Quantitative calibration remains less studied.

location: Main paragraph 9
before: There is also evidence that temporal responses contain useful concentration information. Reservoir computing has tracked changing concentrations despite slow sensor dynamics [8]. More recently, CNN-LSTM models and lightweight transferred networks have supported both recognition and concentration estimation [9], [10]. Small-data transfer and domain-adaptive regression offer further options when calibration data are limited [11], [12].
after: Temporal modeling [8]-[10], small-data transfer [11] and domain-adaptive regression [12] motivate reusable representations for concentration estimation.

location: Main paragraph 10
before: In this work, the sensor array is treated as more than an anonymous multivariate series. Each channel belongs to a physical sensor and may have its own response behavior. Accordingly, a shared temporal encoder learns common dynamics, while sensor identities and cross-sensor attention preserve the organization of the array. Pretraining hides time spans and complete channels, which must be recovered from the remaining measurements. The encoder is later frozen or cautiously fine-tuned for concentration regression. The study tests this approach on two raw-response datasets and across several label budgets. It also follows the public sensor drift dataset into future partitions. We evaluate multi-fold generalization, calibration-design controls, and oracle-class conditional concentration regression under drift, retaining null and adverse comparisons. The complete pipeline is shown in Fig. 1.
after: Our shared temporal encoder learns response dynamics, while sensor identities and cross-sensor attention retain array structure. Masked intervals and channels are reconstructed before frozen or fine-tuned concentration regression. Two raw-response datasets support label-budget and multi-fold evaluation; a descriptor benchmark tests oracle-class regression under future drift. Generic SSL, chemometric, calibration-design and ablation controls retain adverse and null results. Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline.

location: Main paragraph 12
before: Quantitative estimation becomes important when an electronic nose is used as a measuring instrument rather than only as a recognizer. Fonollosa et al. [8] used reservoir computing to estimate rapidly changing concentrations from slower sensor responses. Their study drew attention to transient dynamics, which may be lost when a response is reduced to a steady-state value.
after: Fonollosa et al. [8] used reservoir computing to recover rapidly changing concentrations from slow sensor responses, demonstrating transient information beyond steady-state features.

location: Main paragraph 13
before: Deep models have since combined recognition and regression in several ways. Ni et al. [9] used GAF-MTF representations with a CNN-LSTM model, reporting 95.31% classification accuracy and an R^2 of 0.9510. Tang et al. [10] instead paired a single MEMS sensor with a lightweight transferred network. Work on smaller datasets includes parameter-feature transfer [11], while OT-DARN uses teacher-student domain adaptation with selected pseudo-labels [12].
after: Quantitative models include GAF-MTF/CNN-LSTM feature fusion [9], a lightweight transferred network with a single MEMS sensor [10], small-data parameter-feature transfer [11], and teacher-student domain-adaptive regression [12].

location: Main paragraph 14
before: M-Training [1] and M-S4VMs [2] bring unlabeled samples into electronic nose recognition through predicted labels. This strategy can be helpful when labels are scarce, although incorrect predictions may be reinforced as training continues.
after: M-Training [1] and M-S4VMs [2] use predicted labels for gas recognition, with potential reinforcement of incorrect pseudo-labels.

location: Main paragraph 15

Common time-series objectives include masking, reconstruction, contrastive learning, and adversarial learning [13].
